Figure 2: Architecture of the proposed MICViT. Multiple imaging modalities (e.g., T1, FLAIR, SWI, DWI) are processed via a stem that generates patch embeddings. The model sequentially applies Separated Local (SL) and Separated Global (SG) attention for intra-modality representation learning, followed by Cross Local (CL) and Cross Global (CG) attention to enable explicit cross-modality fusion. Dedicated global query generators are used for SG and CG.

Figure 5: Grad-CAM [63] visualizations for SL, SG, CL, and CG attention across T1, FLAIR, SWI, and DWI, averaged over participants in the UKBB test set. Local and global variants highlight complementary spatial detail and distributed multimodal context.

Figure 3: Illustration of the four attention types operating on latent 3D representations: (a) SL performs local self-attention within spatial windows independently for each modality; (b) SG aggregates global context within each modality via shared global queries; (c) CL applies local cross-attention across modalities within corresponding spatial windows; (d) CG models global cross-modal interactions using shared global queries across modalities.

Table 5: Ablation over single-layer attention permutations on UKBB. We evaluate all combinations of separated local (SL), separated global (SG), cross local (CL), and cross global (CG) attention. The full configuration (SL-SG-CL-CG) achieves the best performance (MAE ↓), consistently outperforming all other permutations. This indicates that gains arise from the interaction of complementary mechanisms rather than any single component. Separated attention (SL, SG) strengthens intra-modality representations, while cross attention (CL, CG) enables inter-modality exchange. Orthogonally, local attention (SL, CL) captures fine-grained structure, whereas global attention (SG, CG) models long-range dependencies.
